opening_line: "Don't mind our website, it's outdated, just call my cell." Your redesign checklist uses that line as the sign a site has outgrown the business.
Your 1% for the Planet post makes the case that good design and good values were never meant to be a trade-off.
Generic websites are basically free now, so real experience gets more valuable, not less. That's the argument in your post on home service marketing going into 2027.
Well-built versus poorly built, not custom versus WordPress. That's how your piece on custom code frames the real comparison.
A beautiful logo is an invitation, but the website is the room people walk into. That's from your post on logos and websites.
The Elo Coffee write-up mentions you don't advertise ecommerce builds and only take them on when it's the right fit.
According to your piece on municipal websites, the best ones aren't the flashiest, they're the ones that help residents find what they need quickly.
Your redesign guide puts lost rankings on the technical side being planned with less care than the visual side, not on good design.
Most lawyer bio pages run on the same template, and adding more adjectives doesn't fix it. That's the point of your piece on attorney bios.
Your Wolverine Construction story says the part of the job you love most is when a company that quietly did the work for years finally gets to be as loud as they deserve.
Your post on environmental consulting websites argues that the firms that get the call aren't the ones with the longest service list, they're the ones that make it easy to see their experience fits.
